papers.title: Osteoporosis Treatment in Lumbar Fusion: A Scoping Review
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed 54 studies on bone-strengthening drugs around lumbar fusion surgery. Most evidence mixed different spine problems together. For short fusions, small teriparatide studies reported less screw loosening and higher or earlier bone union. Evidence for other drugs was thin. This may show patients where bone-health advice still lacks strong proof.

papers.title: Postoperative Complication Timing and Residual Risk after Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion
papers.summary: Researchers studied 112,642 neck fusion surgeries in a national database to see when serious complications happen. They were rare, about 0.9%, and risk fell quickly after surgery. About 43% of bleeding problems with known timing appeared after discharge. This may help families understand when risk is highest, though it sets no discharge times.

papers.title: A bedside score using arrival data to identify major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring fracture: Development and validation
papers.summary: Researchers built a simple bedside score using arrival information to spot severe bleeding after a broken pelvis. Using data from about 240,000 adults, it beat the commonly used shock index. It worked less well after falls and has not been tested in clinics. This points toward faster recognition of dangerous bleeding after injury.

papers.title: Hoxa10 governs lifelong skeletal stem cell maintenance and bone repair
papers.bottomLine: Bone repairs itself because of a reserve of stem cells. This study found that a gene called Hoxa10 helps those stem cells stay in their stem-cell state, and that without it bone heals worse.
takeaways: Removing Hoxa10 in mice gradually depleted skeletal stem cells and impaired bone regeneration.
Hoxa10 also helps organize the collagen scaffold in healing bone.
Lowering related genes in human skeletal stem cells caused similar defects.
papers.technical: Inducible deletion, lineage tracing and single-cell transcriptomics in mice show Hoxa10 restrains premature osteogenic, adipogenic and chondrogenic commitment; effects reproduced by transient distal Hox depletion in primary human SSPCs.
papers.summary: Researchers studied how bone keeps a lifelong reserve of stem cells, which are cells that can build new bone. In mice, losing a gene called Hoxa10 gradually depleted these cells and weakened bone repair. Similar defects appeared in human stem cells. This early lab work may help explain how bones heal and age.

papers.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Open Reduction Internal Fixation Versus Radial Head Arthroplasty for Mason III/IV Radial Head Fractures: A Decision Analytic Markov Model
papers.journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
papers.summary: Researchers used a computer model to compare two treatments for badly broken elbow bones: fixing the pieces with plates and screws, or replacing the radial head with an implant. Under assumed outcomes, replacement looked cost-effective over ten years. The authors stress these assumptions need real-world checks. This may help patients weigh cost and results.

papers.title: Walking the Hemostatic Tightrope in Stroke, VTE, and Orthopedic Surgery: A Scoping Review
papers.summary: Researchers mapped 76 published sources on adults with prior stroke having joint replacement or hip fracture surgery. Most advice on surgery timing, anesthesia and clot-prevention medicine rests on indirect evidence, and no trial compared preventive drugs. Study quality was not rated. This may help explain why plans can differ between patients.

papers.title: Integrating predictive modeling, imaging, and EHR-linked decision support in spine informatics
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed how artificial intelligence is being used in spine care, including reading scans, predicting risks and searching medical records. These tools show promise, but challenges remain, including varied data, privacy and lack of testing in real clinics. Patients may eventually meet such tools, so careful testing before use could help protect them.

papers.title: Fracture orthopedic risk of non-home discharge score II (FORD-II)
papers.summary: Researchers created FORD-II, a score using hospital arrival information to predict which adults with broken bones will need rehab or nursing care instead of going home. Tested on national trauma records, it beat older scores. It needs outside testing. Earlier planning could help families prepare for life after the hospital.

papers.title: The penetrating injury risk of non-home discharge (PIRD) score: Development and validation of a predictive tool using the National Trauma Data Bank
papers.summary: Researchers built the PIRD score to predict which adults with penetrating injuries, such as gunshot or stab wounds, will need rehab or nursing care instead of going home. Using over 300,000 national trauma records, it predicted well. It was tested only on past data. Early prediction could help families plan recovery sooner.

papers.title: Development and validation of the shoulder arthroplasty risk of non-home discharge score: a risk stratification model for non-home discharge following primary total shoulder arthroplasty
papers.journal: Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery
papers.summary: Researchers built a score using only information known before surgery to predict which shoulder replacement patients will not go straight home. Using about 29,000 patients, the score predicted well and beat other tools. It was tested only on past records and needs outside checks. Knowing this earlier may help patients and families plan recovery.

papers.title: Spaceflight drives kidney mitochondrial reprogramming, innate immune activation and suppressed oxidative phosphorylation
papers.summary: Researchers reanalyzed public NASA data on kidney gene activity in female mice flown on three missions. Mitochondria (the cell's energy factories) genes looked less active in some kidneys, mostly after longer flights. Groups had five or six mice, and kidney function was untested. This may help scientists protect astronaut kidneys on long trips.

papers.title: Early Prediction of Mortality and ICU Admission in Trauma Patients Using Machine Learning Models Based on Prehospital and Arrival Data
papers.journal: Journal of the American College of Surgeons
papers.note: Hidden until the DOI is confirmed.

papers.title: Hip Bone Mineral Density Loss Grades with Age and Mission Length in NASA Astronauts
papers.bottomLine: In 94 astronauts (89 with hip data) scanned before and after flight, hip bone density dropped more as age and mission length went up. Spine and whole-body bone did not show the same pattern.
takeaways: The smallest hip loss was about 1.8% (younger astronauts, shorter missions); the largest was about 3.8% (older astronauts, longer missions).
Astronauts were split by age (under or over 45) and mission length (under or over 6 months).
This is an association in a small group, so the authors call for prospective confirmation.
papers.technical: Kruskal-Wallis across four age x duration groups (n = 14, 14, 39, 22) showed a significant hip gradient after Bonferroni correction; spine and whole-body changes were not significant.
papers.summary: Researchers studied 94 astronauts scanned before and after spaceflight, 89 with hip data. Hip bone density loss grew with older age and longer missions, from 1.8% to 3.8%. Spine and whole-body changes were not significant. This association in a small group needs confirmation. It may help guide bone protection for future space travelers.

papers.title: CYP2D6 Metabolizer Phenotype and New Persistent Opioid Use After Spine Surgery
papers.bottomLine: Among 3,820 people who had spine surgery, about 1 in 8 (12.0%) developed new, persistent opioid use. How a person's body breaks down some opioids (a gene called CYP2D6) was linked to that risk, mostly at the extremes.
takeaways: 460 of 3,820 people (12.0%) developed new persistent opioid use after surgery.
Slow metabolizers had about 1.5 times the odds (OR 1.48, 95% CI 1.00-2.18), and the very fast group was similar (OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.89-2.54).
The extreme groups could only be studied in people of European ancestry, so other groups remain unknown.
papers.technical: All of Us retrospective cohort, Firth-penalized logistic regression; overall CYP2D6 association chi-square 15.30, P = .002; poor metabolizers on hydrocodone OR 2.15 (1.07-4.32).
papers.summary: Researchers studied 3,820 adults who had spine surgery and no recent opioid use. About 12% developed new long-term opioid use. How the body breaks down some opioids, a trait set by the CYP2D6 gene, was linked to higher estimated risk at the extremes, though estimates were imprecise. It may someday help personalize pain care.

papers.title: Deep Learning Analysis of Routine Preoperative Knee Radiographs for Five-Year Prediction of Contralateral Arthroplasty
papers.bottomLine: A deep-learning model read routine knee X-rays taken before a knee replacement and predicted which patients would need the other knee done within 5 years. Adding the X-ray to the clinical information did far better than clinical information alone.
takeaways: On 741 test patients (106 had the second surgery), the X-ray-plus-clinical model scored 0.844 versus 0.680 for the clinical-only model.
In exploratory analysis, a frontal film alone scored 0.837 (most patients had only that view).
These are internal results and still need testing at other hospitals.
papers.technical: Multi-view DenseNet121 survival network; 5-year censoring-weighted AUROC 0.844 (X-ray plus clinical model) vs 0.680 (clinical-only; difference 0.164, 0.087 to 0.240). Post hoc, a frontal radiograph alone scored 0.837; 56.6% of patients had only a frontal film.
papers.summary: Researchers trained a computer model to read routine knee X-rays taken before a knee replacement and predict whether the other knee would need replacing within five years. The X-ray added useful information beyond the medical record, mostly from one front-facing view. It needs outside testing. This may someday help patients plan for future care.

papers.title: Response to Letter to the Editor for “Impact of Immunosuppression Type on 30-Day Postoperative Outcomes Following Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion: A Retrospective National Cohort Study of 66,162 Patients”
Cost-Effectiveness of Minimally Invasive Tubular vs. Open Laminectomy for Pure Lumbar Spinal Stenosis: A Markov State-Transition Analysis
papers.summary: Researchers used a computer simulation to compare two back surgeries for spinal narrowing in older adults: minimally invasive tubular surgery and open surgery. Over ten years, the minimally invasive approach cost less and gained slightly more healthy years. This is a model, not a trial. It may inform choices about cost and care.

papers.title: Preoperative Nutritional Optimization in Lumbar Spine Surgery: Associations, Interventions, and Clinical Implications
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed studies on nutrition before lumbar spine surgery. This narrative review had no new patient data. Low albumin and similar markers were linked to more infections and wound problems. One small trial of 103 patients found protein supplements went with fewer complications. Evidence is limited. Good nutrition may help people prepare for back surgery.

papers.title: Response to Comment on “Emergency Department Predictors of Mechanical Ventilation in Pediatric Spine Fracture Patients in the US”
Operative management of traumatic sacral fractures and in-hospital mortality: a national analysis
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed national records of 105,649 adults with a broken sacrum, the bone at the base of the spine. Those who had surgery had lower in-hospital death rates, even after adjusting for differences. This shows an association, not proof that surgery is the cause. It may help patients and surgeons discuss options.

papers.title: Unsupervised Phenotyping of Atrial Fibrillation Using Variational Autoencoders in a Critical Care Cohort: The ATLAS-AF Study
papers.summary: Researchers used a computer learning method to sort 13,967 hospitalized patients with atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, into six groups. Death rates differed across groups, though the groups overlapped and were only moderately repeatable. The findings are early. This may someday help doctors see that one rhythm problem differs between patients.

papers.title: Research priorities in Spine Deformity: a machine learning-based topic analysis of the journal’s first decade (2013–2026)
papers.summary: Researchers used machine learning to read 1,851 abstracts from a spine curvature journal over its first decade. They found 29 research topics. Studies of surgery outcomes, frailty, and large database analyses were growing, and artificial intelligence appeared in under 2% of abstracts. This may help show patients which questions researchers are working on.

papers.title: Neuroimmune Phenotyping as the Next Frontier in Chronic Pain Medicine for Musculoskeletal Back Pain
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed studies linking chronic low back pain to the immune and nervous systems. Pain types seemed to differ in their biology, and ultrasound stiffness measures and some inflammatory markers looked closest to clinical use. Many methods remain experimental and need further trials. This may someday help match back pain treatment to the person.

papers.title: Dynamic simulation and digital twins in atrial fibrillation: Complementary roles and current limitations
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed whether computer simulations and digital twins, which are virtual copies of a patient, could improve care for atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat. Uses so far are mostly early research and procedure planning. These tools have not been proven in routine care. This may help set realistic expectations for personalized heart care.

papers.title: Musculoskeletal degeneration in space: translational parallels with spaceflight-associated ocular pathology and surgical implications
papers.summary: This opinion piece suggests that bone and muscle loss in space and eye changes seen in astronauts may share causes, including fluid shifts and cell energy stress. The authors propose treating them together, with exercise and other countermeasures. These are ideas, not proven findings. They may offer insights for aging and recovery on Earth.

papers.title: Spaceflight induces persistent mitochondrial dysfunction, translational suppression and epigenetic reprogramming in humans
papers.summary: Researchers reanalyzed public data from astronauts on three missions. Right after a short flight, four astronauts' blood immune cells showed lower activity of mitochondria genes (cell energy factories) and protein-building genes. Most changes faded, some lingered. Samples were small, and gene activity does not prove cells worked worse. This may inform future astronaut recovery research.

papers.title: Machine-Learning Augmented Optical Tissue Sensing for Intraoperative Guidance in Spine Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed eight studies of light-based sensors paired with machine learning to tell spine tissues apart, which could help avoid screw misplacement. Across the five studies pooled, accuracy was about 96%, but all were lab, animal or cadaver tissue tests, not living people. This early evidence may someday help make spine surgery safer.

papers.title: Emergency Department Predictors of Mechanical Ventilation in Pediatric Spine Fracture Patients in the US
papers.summary: Researchers studied 29,024 children with spine fractures in a national database. About 20% needed a breathing machine. Low consciousness scores were by far the strongest sign, while low blood pressure and low oxygen also raised the odds. These are associations from past records. Early recognition may help emergency teams and families prepare.

papers.title: Large Language Models in Spine Surgery: A Scoping Review of Clinical Efficacy, Technical Integration, and Ethical Paradigms
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed 15 studies of chatbots and similar large language models in spine surgery. They seemed useful for patient education, documentation and simple triage, but weaker for reading scans and planning surgery. Errors and privacy concerns remain. This may help patients see that these tools could assist, but are no substitute for their doctors.

papers.title: Ordinal Deep Learning for Lumbar Foraminal Stenosis Grading on Sagittal MRI
papers.summary: Researchers trained a computer model to grade narrowing of the nerve openings in the lower spine on MRI scans from 469 patients. The model agreed well with expert grades, and extra measurements did not help. It was tested on a small group and needs outside testing. This may someday help standardize reading of back scans.

papers.title: Impact of Immunosuppression Type on 30-Day Postoperative Outcomes Following Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion: A Retrospective National Cohort Study of 66,162 Patients
papers.summary: Researchers studied 66,162 neck fusion patients in a national database. Those who took corticosteroids before surgery had more infections, readmissions and deaths within 30 days. This is an association from past records. Findings for other immune-suppressing drugs were inconclusive because few patients used them. This may help surgeons weigh steroid use when planning surgery.

papers.title: Preoperative malnutrition is associated with increased early complications and long-term mortality following pilon fracture ORIF: A retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: This retrospective study matched 2,396 pairs of adults after surgery for severe lower leg (pilon) fractures. Malnutrition, defined by low blood markers, was linked to more 90-day readmissions (13.0% vs 6.7%) and two-year deaths (5.2% vs 1.9%). This shows association, not cause. Checking nutrition before surgery may help flag patients needing closer follow-up.

papers.title: Surgical Intervention for Moderate-To-Large lesions (1-2.9 cm 2 ): Proceedings of the International Consensus Meetings on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle
papers.summary: Researchers gathered international ankle experts to agree on surgery for medium and large cartilage damage in the ankle bone. Using a structured voting process, they backed bone grafts for many cases and donor grafts for larger lesions. They noted the evidence is limited. This may help patients understand why surgeons choose different repairs.

papers.title: Early Surgical Decompression and Pulmonary Embolism Risk in Traumatic Cervical Spinal Cord Injury: A Propensity Score-Matched National Analysis
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed records of about 4,500 matched pairs of adults with neck spinal cord injuries. Early surgery within 24 hours was not linked to more lung blood clots. It was linked to higher in-hospital death, which may reflect confounding. This may help families and doctors weigh surgery timing, though more study is needed.

papers.title: Bridging Conservative Management With Injectable Orthobiologic Therapies: Proceedings of the International Consensus Meetings on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle
papers.summary: Seventy-five experts from over 25 countries used a structured voting process to agree on non-surgical care for ankle cartilage injuries. Injections such as platelet-rich plasma were seen as reasonable for some people with lingering symptoms, but no type proved better. This may help patients ask informed questions about their options.

papers.title: Advancing spine connectomics and neural integration through machine learning and neuroengineering: a narrative review
papers.summary: This review summarizes research on how spinal cord circuits work. It suggests the spinal cord does more than relay signals and may adapt movement. Much of the direct evidence still comes from brain studies. The work may eventually help guide treatments for spinal cord injury, such as stimulation and rehabilitation.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Multi-Class Pediatric Wrist Fracture Subtype Classification: A Pilot Study Comparing Convolutional Neural Network Architectures
papers.summary: Researchers tested computer programs that read children's wrist X-rays to name the type of fracture. The best program improved with longer training but was still not accurate enough for clinical use. This is an early step toward tools that might someday help hospitals without bone specialists.

papers.title: The fracture orthopedic risk of non-home discharge (FORD) score: A novel bedside predictive tool for non-home discharge in orthopedic trauma patients
papers.bottomLine: The FORD score uses information available when a fracture patient arrives at the hospital to estimate who is likely to be discharged somewhere other than home. Early flags may help teams plan sooner.
takeaways: Built and tested in 8,422 adults with fractures; 8.1% were not discharged home.
Risk ranged from 1.7% in the lowest group to 34.1% in the highest.
It outperformed two existing trauma scores (AUROC 0.818 versus 0.777 and 0.746).
papers.technical: 15-predictor integer score from logistic regression; validation AUROC 0.818 (95% CI 0.791-0.846); at score >= 4, sensitivity 74.1%, specificity 75.8%, PPV 21.3%, NPV 97.1%.
papers.summary: Researchers built a bedside score using information available at the emergency department to predict which adults with broken bones will not go home. In 8,422 patients at one trauma center, it worked well in testing. Earlier warnings may help families and care teams plan sooner, though it needs further checking elsewhere.

papers.title: Long-term outcomes of lumbar total disc arthroplasty and hybrid constructs: a systematic review
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed 18 studies of 3,346 people who had artificial disc replacement for low back pain, followed five or more years on average. Pain and function stayed improved, and repeat surgery rates were mostly low. It did not clearly prevent later wear in nearby discs. This may help patients weigh motion-preserving surgery.

papers.title: Venous thromboembolism risk in sarcoma patients receiving combined immune checkpoint inhibitors and VEGF pathway inhibitors: a real-world cohort study
papers.summary: Researchers compared sarcoma patients on two cancer drug types versus one. After matching 834 per group, blood clots in one year occurred in 14.0% versus 12.4%. The difference was not statistically clear, and the study was observational. Patients on these drugs may want to ask their care team about clot risk.

papers.title: Response to: comment on ‘digital twins and multimodal artificial intelligence in spine care: a scoping review of concepts, evidence, and translational barriers’
Endoscopic and percutaneous minimally invasive repair of pars interarticularis defects: a systematic review of clinical outcomes
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed five small studies covering 47 patients with a stress fracture in the lower spine, treated with minimally invasive repair. Most bones healed, pain dropped, and about 94% returned to activity. The studies were few and varied. This may help patients considering surgery that avoids spinal fusion.

papers.title: Response to: Comment on ‘Risk prediction in spine surgery: a scoping review of traditional models, artificial intelligence, and the challenge of clinical translation’
Digital twins and multimodal artificial intelligence in spine care: a scoping review of concepts, evidence, and translational barriers
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed 26 studies on digital twins, which are computer models of an individual patient, and artificial intelligence in spine care. Spine digital twins remain mostly an idea, with no proof yet that they improve decisions. Patients may see such tools advertised, so it helps to know the evidence is early.

papers.title: Sequential Versus Step-Therapy Approaches for Osteoporosis Management in Orthopedic Subspecialties
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed 37 studies on two ways to treat weak bones. Starting with bone-building drugs, then bone-protecting ones, generally raised bone density and cut fractures more than the usual step approach. Many fracture patients never get treatment. People with fractures can ask their doctors about bone health.

papers.title: Personalized treatment of chronic tendinopathy using ultrasound and neuroimmune markers: a narrative review
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed studies on chronic tendon pain. This narrative review summarizes existing literature, not new patient data. Shear wave ultrasound detected treatment changes better than standard ultrasound, and pain education plus exercise outperformed exercise alone short-term. The proposed treatment-matching framework is untested and needs trials. It may someday help guide more personalized tendon care.

papers.title: Dynamic spine stabilization through mechanically tuned constructs and embedded biomechanical feedback systems: a narrative review
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed studies of spinal implants that preserve motion and carry built-in sensors. This narrative review summarizes existing literature, not new patient data. Clinical studies were mostly retrospective and modest in size, and tunable, sensor-equipped designs remain early-stage. This research may someday help make back surgery and recovery more personalized.

papers.title: Risk prediction in spine surgery: a scoping review of traditional models, artificial intelligence, and the challenge of clinical translation
papers.summary: Researchers reviewed studies of tools that predict outcomes after spine surgery. Older score-based models predicted fairly well, and artificial intelligence sometimes did slightly better, but not consistently. Testing on new patients and real-world use remain major gaps. This may mean patients are best served treating such predictions as one input, not a guarantee.

papers.title: PRISM-AF: PRIVACY-PRESERVING RISK AND INTERVENTION SYNTHETIC-TWIN SIMULATION MODEL FOR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION MANAGEMENT
papers.rawTitle: PO-FPII-036 PRISM-AF: PRIVACY-PRESERVING RISK AND INTERVENTION SYNTHETIC-TWIN SIMULATION MODEL FOR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION MANAGEMENT

papers.title: Primary Tibiotalocalcaneal Nailing vs Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Fragility Ankle Fractures in Older Adults: A Markov Model
papers.summary: Researchers used a computer model to compare two surgeries for ankle fractures in people aged 75 and older. Standard plate and screw surgery cost less, with nearly identical quality of life. The model relied on published estimates, not new patients. This may help older adults and families discuss surgical options.

papers.title: Perioperative ischemic optic neuropathy: a comprehensive review of anesthetic implications, hemodynamic pathophysiology, and risk stratification
papers.summary: This review explains why a few people lose vision after surgery not involving the eyes, most often spine or heart operations. It points to poor blood flow to the optic nerve, linked to low blood pressure, long prone surgeries, and swelling. Knowing the risks may help patients talk with their surgical and anesthesia teams.

papers.title: Endoscopic versus open lumbar decompression: a retrospective cohort study of 31,000 patients with 90-day follow-up
papers.bottomLine: Researchers compared endoscopic (keyhole) and open lumbar decompression in 31,408 matched pairs of patients. Endoscopic surgery had fewer spinal-fluid leaks and repeat operations, but a few other complications were slightly more common.
takeaways: Unplanned reoperation within 90 days: 0.2% with endoscopic versus 1.8% with open surgery.
Meningitis, blood clots in the leg and heart attacks were somewhat more frequent after endoscopic surgery.
The absolute differences were small, and this was a database study rather than a trial.
papers.technical: TriNetX retrospective cohort, 1:1 propensity matching (31,408 per arm); durotomy 0.4% vs 0.4%; CSF leak or pseudomeningocele 0.3% vs 0.5%; healthcare utilization 6.3% vs 6.1%.
papers.summary: Researchers compared keyhole and open back surgery for nerve pressure in 31,408 matched pairs of patients. Keyhole surgery had fewer spinal fluid leaks and repeat operations. Meningitis, clots, and heart attacks were slightly more common after keyhole surgery. This retrospective study may help patients weigh surgical options, though it cannot prove cause.

papers.title: A Validated Transcriptomic NMJ Remodeling Score Reveals Synaptic Dysfunction Independent of Muscle Atrophy after Immobilization in a Microgravity Analog
papers.summary: Researchers built a gene activity score for the connection between nerves and muscles. In adults whose leg was immobilized for 10 days, the score rose and partly recovered, separately from muscle shrinkage. This suggests nerves may contribute to weakness. It may someday help doctors understand why a limb feels weak after time in a cast.

papers.title: Spaceflight is associated with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation suppression and immune dysregulation that persist after return: a cross-mission transcriptomic analysis
papers.summary: Researchers combined gene activity data from 70 spaceflight comparisons across 21 tissues, including mouse studies. Genes for cell energy production were turned down in flight, more so with higher radiation, and stayed low after return in high-exposure datasets. It may help keep future space travelers healthy on long missions.
